mainTopic: When words of length make one term of נזירות, many terms, or just thirty days; and why adding a day or an hour makes two terms
overview: The amud opens by finishing an earlier discussion. Years are counted by months, not days, as the רבנן of קיסרי learn from a פסוק. A new משנה then rules that 'one long term,' 'one short term,' or even 'from now until the end of the world' gives only thirty days of נזירות, because he only means it feels that long. The גמרא challenges this from the משנה of 'from here until such and such a place,' which counts the real travel days. רבא answers that there the man was already on the road. The גמרא then asks why each פרסה or lodging station is not its own term, as with 'like the dust of the earth.' The answers given are that people there don't count פרסאות, that things with a fixed amount differ from endless ones, and (רבה) that hairs are separate while days and roads are continuous. רבא then says all of this is unnecessary, since our משנה says 'one.' Finally, a new משנה rules that adding a day, an hour, or a half makes two full terms, and the גמרא explains why each example is needed.

steps.title: Maybe it means a year
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests that the earlier phrase could refer to a year rather than a month.
steps.simpleTranslation: But say it is talking about a year!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is continuing an earlier discussion and challenges it. It suggests that what was explained as a month could just as well be a year.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier discussion said the words refer to a month, because a month can be 'full' or 'lacking' by one day. The challenge is that a year can also be longer or shorter, so why not read it as a year?

keyTerms.meaning: But say / why not say (a suggestion of another reading)

phrases.english: But say it is a year?
phrases.notes: Earlier the גמרא said these words were talking about a month; now it asks, why not a year?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the earlier סוגיא from the previous amud.
steps.kashyaTarget: The earlier reading that the phrase refers to a month.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A year can also be longer or shorter, so the phrase could refer to a year just as well.

steps.title: Years are not counted by days
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that we do not count days toward a year.
steps.simpleTranslation: Do we count years by days?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the suggestion with a sharp question: years are not measured in days.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Calling something 'full' or 'lacking' by one day only works for a unit that is counted in days. A month is counted that way, but a year is not, so the phrase cannot be talking about a year.

keyTerms.meaning: Do we count? (a question that means 'we certainly do not')

phrases.english: Do we count by days?!
phrases.notes: He means: do we count years by days? The answer is obviously no.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge from step 1.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rejects the alternative reading on principle.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The phrase could be about a year, since years also vary in length.
steps.terutzMaskana: Years are not counted in days, so the phrase must be about a month.

steps.title: Proof from the Sages of Caesarea
steps.stepSummary: The רבנן of קיסרי learn from the פסוק 'לחדשי השנה' that years are made of months, not days.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Sages of Caesarea said: From where do we know that we do not count days toward years? Because it says 'of the months of the year.' Months are counted toward years, but days are not.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a source to back up the answer in step 2.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק links 'months' directly to 'the year.' From this the רבנן of קיסרי learn that a year is built out of months, and single days do not count toward it. This supports the claim that a year is not measured in days.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Of the months of the year' (the פסוק)

steps.whatToRemember: Years are counted by months, not by days. So 'full' or 'lacking' by a day only fits a month.

phrases.english: But didn't the Sages of Caesarea say:
From where do we know that we do not count days toward years?
As it is said: 'Of the months of the year.'
Months are counted toward years,
but days are not counted toward years.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the answer of step 2 with a teaching based on a פסוק.
steps.raayaObject: That years are not counted by days.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The teaching of the רבנן of קיסרי from 'לחדשי השנה' (שמות 12:2).

steps.title: משנה: long, short, or until the end of the world means thirty days
steps.stepSummary: Someone who says he is a נזיר for 'one long' term, 'one short' term, or even 'from now until the end of the world' is a נזיר for thirty days.
steps.simpleTranslation: If someone said: 'I am a נזיר for one long term,' or 'I am a נזיר for one short term,' or even 'from now until the end of the world,' he is a נזיר for thirty days.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It rules that vague words about length, even very dramatic ones, still give only a standard thirty-day נזירות.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Words like 'long' or 'short' do not set an actual number of days, so the default נזירות of thirty days applies. The word 'even' shows that 'until the end of the world' is the most surprising case, since it sounds like forever.

keyTerms.meaning: Thirty days, the standard length of a נזירות

steps.whatToRemember: A vague description of length, even 'until the end of the world,' gives only the standard thirty days.

phrases.english: MISHNAH:
If he said: 'I am hereby a nazirite for one long [term],'
phrases.notes: The word 'term' is not in the text, but it is what he means.

phrases.english: or 'I am hereby a nazirite for one short [term],'
even 'from now until the end of the world':
he is a nazirite for thirty days.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְנִי׳ אָמַר הֲרֵינִי נָזִיר אַחַת גְּדוֹלָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new משנה; the earlier סוגיא has ended.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Vague descriptions of length, including 'from now until the end of the world,' produce a thirty-day נזירות.

steps.title: Why only thirty days if he said forever?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why 'until the end of the world' gives only thirty days, when he seems to mean forever.
steps.simpleTranslation: Why? Didn't he say 'from now until the end of the world'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the last case in the משנה. His words seem to mean a lifelong נזירות.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Long' and 'short' are vague, but 'until the end of the world' sounds like a clear and endless time. So it is puzzling that the משנה gives the shortest standard term.

phrases.english: GEMARA:
Why?
But he said 'from now until the end of the world'!

steps.triggerLanguage: אַמַּאי וְהָא מִכָּאן וְעַד סוֹף הָעוֹלָם קָאָמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the last ruling of the משנה in step 4.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ruling that 'until the end of the world' means thirty days.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: His words seem to describe an endless time, so he should be a נזיר forever, not just thirty days.

steps.title: He means it feels that long
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains that he meant the נזירות feels as long to him as until the end of the world.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is what he is saying: This matter feels as long to me as from now until the end of the world.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers by reading his words as an expression of feeling, not as a length of time.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He was not setting how long the נזירות lasts. He was saying how hard and drawn-out it will feel. Since he named no real length, the default of thirty days applies.

keyTerms.meaning: This is what he is saying (rereading someone's words)

steps.confusionAlert: He is not accepting a lifelong נזירות. 'Until the end of the world' describes how the thirty days feel to him, not how long they last.

phrases.english: This is what he is saying:
This matter is as long for me
phrases.notes: 'This matter' is the נזירות he is taking on.

phrases.english: as from now until the end of the world.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָכִי קָאָמַר אֲרִיכָא לִי הָדָא מִילְּתָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 5.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'Until the end of the world' sets a lifelong term.
steps.terutzMaskana: It describes how long the נזירות feels, so only thirty days apply.

steps.title: Challenge from 'until such and such a place'
steps.stepSummary: A later משנה measures 'from here until a certain place' literally. Why not say there too that he only means it feels that long?
steps.simpleTranslation: We learned: 'I am a נזיר from here until such and such a place.' We estimate how many days it takes from here to that place. If it is less than thirty days, he is a נזיר for thirty days. If not, he is a נזיר for that number of days. But say here too: this matter feels as long to me as from here until that place!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer from step 6 by quoting another משנה, where a distance is taken literally as a number of days.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If dramatic words can mean 'it feels long to me,' then 'from here until such and such a place' could mean the same thing and give only thirty days. Yet that משנה actually counts the travel days. That suggests people's words of distance or time are taken at face value.

keyTerms.meaning: According to the number of days

phrases.english: We learned:
'I am hereby a nazirite from here until such and such a place':
we estimate how many days [it takes]
from here until such and such a place.
If it is less than thirty days,
he is a nazirite for thirty days.
And if not,
phrases.notes: He means: if the trip takes more than thirty days.

phrases.english: he is a nazirite for the number of days.
But say here too:
This matter is as long for me
as from here until such and such a place!

steps.triggerLanguage: תְּנַן הֲרֵינִי נָזִיר מִכָּאן עַד מָקוֹם פְּלוֹנִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer of step 6 by comparing it to another משנה.
steps.kashyaTarget: The reading 'it feels this long to me' given in step 6.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If that reading works for 'until the end of the world,' it should also work for 'until such and such a place.' But that משנה counts the actual days, so this kind of language is taken literally.
steps.whyThisMatters: This forces the גמרא to explain how to tell when a person's words set a real length of time and when they only express feeling.

steps.title: He had already set out on the road
steps.stepSummary: רבא explains that the משנה of 'from here until a certain place' is talking about someone who had already started traveling, so his words obviously refer to the actual trip.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: The משנה is talking about someone who had already set out on the road.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא answers the question from Step 7: why is 'from here until a certain place' taken literally? Because the man was already on the road when he said it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Saying 'until the end of the world' can't be about real travel, so we read it as 'it feels that long.' But a man who is already walking toward a place and names that place clearly means the real trip. His situation shows what he means.

keyTerms.meaning: An אמורא who gives the answer here
Set out on the road, already started the journey

phrases.english: Rava said:
It is where he had already set out on the road.
phrases.notes: He is explaining the later משנה from Step 7: the man was already walking toward that place when he spoke.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of Step 7
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limits the case: the משנה is about someone already traveling
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'Until a certain place' might mean 'it feels as long as that trip,' just like 'until the end of the world'
steps.terutzMaskana: Since he was already on the road, he clearly means the real trip, so it is measured literally

steps.title: Why not a separate term for every פרסה?
steps.stepSummary: If he means the real trip, why not treat every פרסה of the trip as its own term of נזירות?
steps.simpleTranslation: But then let each and every פרסה count as a separate term of נזירות!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on רבא's answer. If the trip is measured in פרסאות, maybe he took on one term for each פרסה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה treats the whole trip as one long term. The challenge is that a trip is made of measured units, so maybe each unit should be its own term. That would give him many separate terms instead of one.

keyTerms.meaning: A measure of distance (a parasang), used for travel

phrases.english: And let each and every parasang be a separate term!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבא's answer in Step 8
steps.kashyaTarget: Treating the whole journey as one single term of נזירות
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the trip is measured in units, each unit could be read as its own term

steps.title: A place where people don't count in פרסאות
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא answers that the משנה is talking about a place where people do not measure distance in פרסאות.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: The משנה is talking about a place where people do not count distances in פרסאות.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא answers the challenge: in that place nobody thinks of the trip in פרסאות, so there are no units to split it into.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A speaker is judged by how people around him talk. If the local people don't divide trips into פרסאות, the man had no such units in mind. He meant the whole trip as one term.

keyTerms.meaning: An אמורא who gives this answer

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said:
It is in a place where they do not count parasangs.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב פָּפָּא: בְּאַתְרָא דְּלָא מָנֵי פַּרְסֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of Step 9
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limits the case to a place without that unit of measure
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Each פרסה might be its own term
steps.terutzMaskana: Where people don't count פרסאות, the trip is one single term

steps.title: Why not a separate term for every lodging station?
steps.stepSummary: Even without פרסאות, trips have stopping stations. The גמרא uses a משנה to show that a number-like expression can make many terms, so why not one term per station?
steps.simpleTranslation: But then let each and every lodging station count as a separate term! Didn't we learn in a משנה: If someone says, 'I am a נזיר like the dust of the earth,' or 'like the hair of my head,' or 'like the sand of the sea,' he is a נזיר עולם and shaves once every thirty days?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks again: every trip has stations where travelers stop for the night, so count one term per station. It supports this with a משנה where a word like 'dust' makes many separate terms.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the משנה, 'like the dust of the earth' is read as one term per grain, so he keeps finishing thirty-day terms and shaving. By the same logic, a trip with stations should mean one term per station. The challenge is that we already know words can split into many terms.

keyTerms.meaning: A lodging station where travelers stop for the night
Didn't we learn in a משנה?
A permanent נזיר, one whose נזירות goes on forever
Shaves (at the end of a term of נזירות)

phrases.english: And let each and every way station be a separate term!
Didn't we learn in a mishna:
phrases.notes: This משנה comes later, on דף ח.

phrases.english: "I am hereby a nazirite like the dust of the earth,"
or "like the hair of my head," or "like the sand of the sea":
he is a permanent nazirite,
and he shaves once every thirty days?!
phrases.notes: He takes on one term per grain or hair, so every thirty days a term ends and he shaves.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְלִיהְוֵי כׇּל אַוּוֹנָא וְאַוּוֹנָא! מִי לָא תְּנַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new challenge after רב פפא's answer in Step 10, backed by a משנה
steps.kashyaTarget: Treating the whole journey as one term, even where פרסאות aren't counted
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Stations still divide the trip, and the משנה shows that wording like 'dust' or 'hair' turns into many separate terms

steps.title: Things with a fixed amount are different
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the משנה of 'dust, hair, and sand' doesn't include anything that has a fixed, countable amount.
steps.simpleTranslation: Anything that has a fixed amount is not taught in that משנה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why the trip is different from 'dust of the earth.' The משנה only means endless things, not things with a set amount.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Dust, hair, and sand feel countless, so the speaker can't mean one term of that size, and we read it as many terms. A trip has a set length with a clear end, so he means one term as long as that trip. The difference is endless versus fixed.

keyTerms.meaning: It does not teach (it isn't included)

steps.whatToRemember: Words that describe something endless (dust, sand, hair) become many separate terms of נזירות. Something with a set measure, like a known trip, becomes one long term.

phrases.english: Anything that has a fixed amount
is not taught there.
phrases.notes: He means the משנה of dust, hair and sand only covers things people think of as countless.

steps.triggerLanguage: כׇּל מִילְּתָא דְּאִית בַּיהּ קִיצּוּתָא לָא קָתָנֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of Step 11
steps.terutzResolutionType: Draws a distinction between endless things and things with a fixed measure
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A trip with stations should split into many terms, like dust or sand
steps.terutzMaskana: Only endless things split into many terms; a fixed trip is one long term

steps.title: A ברייתא: a fixed number of years is not נזיר עולם
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא supports the difference between fixed and endless: 'all my life' makes a נזיר עולם, but even a thousand fixed years is just a נזיר whose term never ends.
steps.simpleTranslation: And so it was taught in a ברייתא: If someone says, 'I am a נזיר all the days of my life,' or 'I am a נזיר עולם,' he is a נזיר עולם. But even if he says a hundred years, or even a thousand years, he is not a נזיר עולם. He is a נזיר forever.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that shows the same idea. A fixed amount of time, however huge, is treated differently from a term with no limit.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A thousand years is longer than his whole life, yet because it is a set number, he is not a נזיר עולם. He is a regular נזיר whose term never runs out in his lifetime. This matches Step 12: a fixed measure is one long term, not the special endless category.

keyTerms.meaning: And it was taught in a ברייתא (bringing support)
All the days of my life
A regular נזיר whose term just never ends

steps.confusionAlert: נְזִיר עוֹלָם and נָזִיר לְעוֹלָם sound almost the same but are different categories. The first is the special permanent נזיר; the second is a regular נזיר with an endless term.
steps.whatToRemember: Fixed time, even a thousand years, makes a regular נזיר whose term never ends. Only an open-ended expression like 'all my life' makes a נזיר עולם.

phrases.english: And so it is taught in a baraita:
"I am hereby a nazirite all the days of my life,"
or "I am hereby a permanent nazirite":
he is a permanent nazirite.

phrases.aramaic: אֲפִילּוּ מֵאָה שָׁנָה, אֲפִילּוּ אֶלֶף שָׁנִים —
phrases.english: Even if he said one hundred years, even one thousand years,
he is not a permanent nazirite,
rather, he is a nazirite forever.
phrases.notes: He's a regular נזיר; his term just won't end before he dies.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָתַנְיָא: הֲרֵינִי נָזִיר כׇּל יְמֵי חַיַּי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the distinction made in Step 12
steps.raayaObject: The idea that a fixed measure is treated differently from an endless one
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא contrasting 'all my life' (נזיר עולם) with a fixed number of years (נזיר לעולם)

steps.title: רבה: hairs are separate units
steps.stepSummary: רבה gives a different reason why hair and dust create many terms of נזירות while a trip does not: each hair stands apart from the next.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה said: Hairs are different, because each one is separate from the other.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה offers another answer to the question of why a trip doesn't become many terms of נזירות, one for each station.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Before this, the difference was 'fixed amount' versus 'endless amount'. רבה uses a new idea: hairs are physically separate, one by one, so each one can stand for its own term. A road has no natural breaks, so it stays one term.

phrases.english: Rabba said:
Hairs are different,
since they are separated one from another.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second answer to the question in step 11, different from the 'fixed versus endless' answer in steps 12-13.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Different reason: separate units versus one continuous whole
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Any number-like expression, such as stations on a trip, should make many terms of נזירות.
steps.terutzMaskana: Only things made of naturally separate units, like hairs, make many terms. A continuous road makes one term.

steps.title: But days are also separate units
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רבה: days are also separate units, as the פסוק says 'evening and morning, one day', so a trip of many days should make many terms.
steps.simpleTranslation: With days too, isn't it written: 'And there was evening and there was morning, one day'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks רבה's answer, saying that days are also separate units, just like hairs.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If separate units make separate terms, then a trip that takes several days should count one term for each day. The פסוק seems to show that each day is its own closed unit.

phrases.english: With regard to days too,
isn't it written:
"And there was evening and there was morning, one day"!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבה's 'separate units' idea from step 14.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבה's claim that only separate units create separate terms
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Days are also separate units according to the פסוק, so a trip lasting days should make one term per day.

steps.title: The verse only defines a day; time is continuous
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the פסוק does not mean days are cut off from each other. It only teaches that a day and a night together count as one day.
steps.simpleTranslation: There, it does not mean that days are separate from each other. What is it saying? That daytime and nighttime together are one day, but really days are never separated from each other.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רבה by explaining what the פסוק really means.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק is only defining how long one day is: night plus day. It does not say there is a break between one day and the next. Time keeps flowing, so it is continuous like a road, not separate like hairs.

phrases.english: There, it is not that they are cut off from each other.
What is it saying?
Daytime and nighttime are one day,
but really they are not cut off from each other.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 15 and saves רבה's answer.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The פסוק shows that each day is a separate, closed unit.
steps.terutzMaskana: The פסוק only defines a day as night plus day. Time is continuous, so days don't make separate terms of נזירות.
steps.whatToRemember: According to רבה, hairs make many terms because each hair is separate. Roads and days are continuous, so they make only one term.

steps.title: רבא: the vow said 'one'
steps.stepSummary: רבא says all these questions were unnecessary, because in the משנה the person said 'I am a נזיר one time', so it is clearly one term.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: Why do you need to raise all these difficulties? It is different there, because the משנה teaches that he said 'I am hereby a נזיר one time.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבא steps back from the whole discussion, which began with the question of step 5 on the 'until the end of the world' case. He gives a much simpler answer based on the wording of our משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier answer, 'it feels that long to me', led to a series of challenges and defenses. רבא says none of that is needed. Our משנה (step 4) has the person say 'I am a נזיר one,' so his words cannot be read as many terms or as an endless נזירות. They describe a single term, and that term is the standard thirty days.

keyTerms.meaning: I am hereby a נזיר one time

steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up רבה (step 14) and רבא (this step). They are two different אמוראים giving two different answers.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that a person's exact words in a vow decide its meaning: saying 'one' locks in a single term, no matter how long it lasts.

phrases.english: Rava said:
Why do you need to raise all these difficulties?
It is different there,
phrases.notes: "There" means the case in the משנה of a person who vowed to be a נזיר from here until the end of the world.

phrases.english: since it teaches: "I am hereby a nazir one time."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Steps back from the whole discussion (steps 6-16) and answers the original question of step 5 about the 'until the end of the world' case in a simpler way.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reading the exact wording of the משנה
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We needed to read 'until the end of the world' as 'it feels that long to me.' That reading then forced special answers to the challenges that followed.
steps.terutzMaskana: The משנה says he vowed 'one', so he took on a single term. It is neither many terms nor a נזירות without end, and it is the standard thirty days.

steps.title: Adding a day, an hour, or a half means two terms
steps.stepSummary: The משנה rules that 'I am a נזיר and one day,' 'and one hour,' or 'one and a half' all make the person a נזיר for two terms.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: If someone says 'I am a נזיר and one day,' or 'I am a נזיר and one hour,' or 'I am a נזיר one and a half,' he is a נזיר for two terms.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה starts. It gives three ways of adding a small extra amount to a נזירות vow, and says all of them lead to two terms.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Saying 'I am a נזיר' means one term of thirty days. Any extra amount on top of that, even a tiny one, cannot be a short נזירות of its own, so it becomes a whole second term.
steps.confusionAlert: He does not keep thirty days plus one day or one hour. The small addition turns into a complete second term.

phrases.english: MISHNAH
"I am hereby a nazir and one day,"
"I am hereby a nazir and one hour,"
"I am hereby a nazir one and a half"
he is a nazir for two.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה after the discussion of 'one time' ended in Step 17.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Any addition to a basic נזירות vow, such as a day, an hour, or a half, creates a second full term.

steps.title: Why list so many cases?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the משנה needs all three examples instead of just one.
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: Why does the משנה need to teach all of these cases?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens by asking why the משנה gives several examples of the same rule. This question sets up the explanation in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: All three cases seem to teach one idea: an addition makes two terms. The גמרא wants to know what each example adds that the others do not.

phrases.english: GEMARA
Why do I need to teach all these?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks about the wording of the משנה from Step 18.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What each of the several cases in the משנה teaches that one case alone would not.

steps.title: The day case alone would not teach the hour case
steps.stepSummary: The cases are needed. From 'one day' alone, someone might think two terms apply only because a day is too short for נזירות, while an extra hour would just add one more day.
steps.simpleTranslation: They are needed. If the משנה taught only 'I am a נזיר and one day,' I would say that only here two terms apply, because there is no נזירות for one day. But for 'I am a נזיר and one hour,' I might say he should count thirty-one days. So the משנה teaches us that this case is also two terms.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the cases are not extra. Each one blocks a mistake someone could make from the other.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With 'one day,' the reason for two terms seems clear: a one-day נזירות does not exist. With 'one hour,' a person might think the hour simply stretches the term by one day, giving thirty-one days. The משנה lists the hour case to show that it is also two full terms.

keyTerms.meaning: there is no נזירות for one day

steps.whatToRemember: Even a tiny addition like one hour does not just lengthen the term. It creates a whole second term of נזירות.
